summary: Specifies the Time protocol, which gives a site-independent, machine readable date and time as seconds since midnight on January first 1900. It is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 868 defines the Time Protocol, a simple service that tells a requesting computer what time it is. The answer is one number: the seconds elapsed since midnight on 1 January 1900 GMT. A computer without a clock, or with a doubtful one, can ask several time servers and check its own clock against theirs.

subtitle: A service on port 37 that returns the time as a 32-bit count of seconds since 1900.

tldr.problem: Not every system has a clock, and all clocks can be wrong, so hosts need a way to confirm or correct their idea of the time from independent sites.
tldr.mechanism: A server on port 37 returns a 32-bit binary number: the seconds since midnight on 1 January 1900 GMT, either after a TCP connection or as one UDP reply to an empty datagram.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it, and the RFC notes the 1900 base will serve until the year 2036.

today: RFC 868 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the Time Protocol.

sections.title: A Machine-Readable Time Service
sections.content:
The Time Protocol provides a site-independent, machine readable date and time. The Time service sends back to the originating source the time in seconds since midnight on 1 January 1900.

One motivation is that not all systems have a date/time clock, and all are subject to occasional human or machine error. Time servers make it possible to quickly confirm or correct a system's idea of the time by making a brief poll of several independent sites on the network. The protocol may be used either above the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) or above the User Datagram Protocol (UDP).
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers have no clock, and every clock can drift. This service answers one question, what time is it, with a single number any computer can read.

sections.title: Using TCP and UDP
sections.content:
Over TCP the service works as follows. The server listens on port 37 (45 octal). The user connects to port 37. The server sends the time as a 32-bit binary number, and the user receives it; then the user closes the connection and the server closes the connection. If the server is unable to determine the time at its site, it should either refuse the connection or close it without sending anything.

Over UDP the service works as follows. The server listens on port 37. The user sends an empty datagram to port 37. The server receives it and sends back a datagram containing the time as a 32-bit binary number. If the server is unable to determine the time, it should discard the arriving datagram and make no reply.
sections.plainLanguage: Over TCP the server sends the number once and hangs up. Over UDP the client sends an empty message and the server answers with one message carrying the number. A server that does not know the time stays silent.

sections.title: The Time Value
sections.content:
The time is the number of seconds since 00:00 (midnight) 1 January 1900 GMT, such that the time 1 is 12:00:01 am on 1 January 1900 GMT. The RFC states that this base will serve until the year 2036.

The RFC's own examples: the time 2,208,988,800 corresponds to 00:00 1 Jan 1970 GMT; 2,398,291,200 to 00:00 1 Jan 1976 GMT; 2,524,521,600 to 00:00 1 Jan 1980 GMT; and 2,629,584,000 to 00:00 1 May 1983 GMT. The value -1,297,728,000 corresponds to 00:00 17 Nov 1858 GMT.
sections.plainLanguage: The number counts every second since the start of 1900. Large numbers mean later times, and the RFC says this counting scheme lasts until 2036.
